lines.cap: **Narrator:** Term 2. Room 8H. Mug number nine. Today, Year 8 begins **Poetry**.
**Will:** Finally! **154** sonnets, published in **1609** — every single one a masterpiece by me!
**Mr H:** And Blake, Dickinson, Wordsworth, Rossetti, Tennyson, Keats, and Wilfred Owen.
**Will:** **Wordsworth**?! The man wandered lonely as a cloud! Where are the sword fights?!
**Mei:** Poetry's easy! 'Tennyson uses a metaphor, "like a thunderbolt", which makes the reader want to read on.'
**Nib:** She wrote 'makes the reader want to read on'! Fetch a blotter, I am haemorrhaging ink!
**Simile:** Excuse me?! 'Like a thunderbolt' has **LIKE** right in front of it! That's **me** — **Simile**!
**Metaphor:** And I am **Metaphor**! Simile says he is *like* a lion; **I AM a lion**! We are NOT twins!
**Mei:** Term 2 Poetry: **one star**. Too many loud relatives.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode seven: Simile Is Not Like a Metaphor.
**Mr H:** A poem is a machine for making meaning. Just naming a gear is **feature spotting** — it earns almost nothing.
**Nib:** Travel the whole chain — **WHAT? HOW? WHY?**: **Technique + short embedded Evidence + Effect + Meaning**!
**Mr H:** Zoom in on one word's **connotations** — its associations beyond the dictionary — and link to the **theme**.
**Mei:** So when the poet says 'I', I write what the poet was feeling that Tuesday?
**Nib:** Trap! The '**I**' is the **speaker** or **persona**, not automatically the poet! Remember: **the poet chooses, the speaker says**.
**Mr H:** In Browning's **dramatic monologue** *My Last Duchess*, a jealous Duke speaks to a silent listener — Browning wasn't a murderer.
**Nib:** Distinguish **tone** — the speaker's attitude, like *wistful*, *awed*, or *bitter* — from **mood**, the atmosphere the reader feels.
**Mei:** Like that Singapore poem *Monsoon, Four O'Clock*! Over Toa Payoh the sky 'clenches like a fist', then under the HDB void deck the storm becomes 'an old friend'!
**Mr H:** Checklist any unseen poem with **SMILE**: **Structure, Meaning, Imagery, Language, Effect** — with **Effect** in every sentence.
**Narrator:** Library. Metaphor and Simile are still refusing to share a chair.
**Simile:** Watch the badge! A **simile** compares two things using '**like**' or '**as**', keeping them separate: Tennyson's eagle 'like a thunderbolt he falls'!
**Metaphor:** A **metaphor** is bolder — it fuses them! Blake's 'Tyger Tyger, **burning bright**' turns stripes straight into fire!
**Metaphor:** Stretch me across a whole poem and I'm an **extended metaphor**! Emily Dickinson wrote nearly **1,800** poems — and turned hope into a bird!
**Mei:** '"Hope" is the thing with **feathers** - / That **perches** in the soul -'. 'Feathers' connotes softness and flight, yet this tiny bird survives the gale!
**Nib:** **Personification** gives human actions to the non-human: in Tennyson's *The Eagle*, 'The **wrinkled** sea beneath him **crawls**', shrinking the ocean into something old and weak.
**Nib:** **Pathetic fallacy** is weather or nature mirroring human emotion: Keats's 'The sedge has withered from the lake, / And no birds sing' mirrors despair.
**Mr H:** Add **symbolism** — Blake's Lamb for innocence — and a **semantic field**: words from one area, like *hammer, chain, furnace, anvil* in *The Tyger*.
**Mei:** Okay, zooming in on 'feathers' actually made sense. **Two and a half stars**!

chapters.title: Sound: poems are made to be heard

lines.cap: **Mr H:** Poems began as song. Always mouth a poem silently in an exam so you **hear** what the sounds do.
**Mei:** Any repeated letter anywhere is **alliteration**, right?
**Nib:** No, darling! **Alliteration** is repeated consonant sounds at the **start** of nearby words: 'He **c**lasps the **c**rag with **c**rooked hands' — hard talons gripping rock!

**Nib:** Repeated **vowel** sounds inside words are **assonance** — Poe's 'm**e**llow w**e**dding b**e**lls' — while inner or final consonants are **consonance**, like 'bla**ck**, cra**ck**ed ro**ck**s'.
**Simile:** **Sibilance** repeats *s* or *sh* sounds! It can be a gentle sea whisper **or** sinister — Owen's '**s**hrill, demented choirs of wailing **sh**ells'! Always say which!
**Metaphor:** **Plosives** — *p, b, t, d, k, g* — explode off the lips! And **onomatopoeia** imitates the sound itself!
**Mr H:** Hear Wilfred Owen stack them all: 'Only the s**t**u**tt**ering **r**ifles' **r**apid **r**a**tt**le' — alliteration, onomatopoeia, and harsh *t* plosives firing like a machine gun.
**Mr H:** **Rhythm** is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables; regular rhythm is **metre**, measured in **feet**.
**Mei:** Memory trick! **An iamb runs a-WAY** — da-DUM! **A trochee is a TI-ger** — DUM-da!
**Will:** My turn! Five iambs make **iambic pentameter**: 'Shall I com-PARE thee TO a SUM-mer's DAY?' Steady as a heartbeat!
**Mr H:** Four feet make **tetrameter** — Wordsworth's gentle 'I WAN-dered LONE-ly AS a CLOUD' — while Blake's trochaic 'TY-ger TY-ger' hammers like a forge, and **anapaests** gallop!
**Nib:** Now **rhyme**: **full rhyme** matches cleanly (*trees / breeze*); **half** or **slant rhyme** (*soul / all*) feels uneasy and unfinished; **internal rhyme** chimes mid-line.
**Will:** And mind historical pronunciation! Blake's *eye* and *symmetry* looks like an **eye rhyme** today, though Georgian Londoners often rhymed it!
**Simile:** Label a **rhyme scheme** with letters! Wordsworth's *Daffodils* goes **ABABCC** — closing each stanza on a neat **rhyming couplet**!
**Mei:** Three and a half stars. Don't tell Will, his head won't fit through the library door.
**Mr H:** *Stanza* is Italian for 'room'. Count lines from two to eight: **Cool Tigers Quietly Creep, Silently Stalking Owls** — couplet, tercet, quatrain, cinquain, sestet, septet, octave.
**Nib:** **End-stopped** lines pause with punctuation at the end; **enjambment** spills the sentence straight over the line break without pausing!
**Kevin:** And a pause right **inside** a line is a **caesura**! Edward Thomas writes 'Yes. I remember Adlestrop—' and Wordsworth's dashes make you stop and gaze with me!
**Volta:** Stand back — **VOLTA** incoming! Italian for **turn**! Whenever a poem flips mood or argument on '**Yet**' or '**But**', that's me!
**Volta:** A **Petrarchan sonnet** has an eight-line **octave** (ABBAABBA) and six-line **sestet**, turning at **line 9** — like Rossetti's *Remember*!
**Nib:** Rossetti begs 'Remember me', turns on '**Yet**', and closes tenderly: 'Better by far you should forget and smile / Than that you should remember and be sad.'
**Will:** Whereas my **Shakespearean sonnet** has **three quatrains** and a final **rhyming couplet** — ABAB CDCD EFEF GG — saving the knockout turn for **line 13**!

**Mr H:** Know **ballad**, **elegy**, **ode**, **haiku**, **villanelle**, **cyclical structure** — Blake changing 'Could frame' to '**Dare** frame' — and **free verse**: no fixed rhyme or metre, yet **deliberate** line breaks!
**Mei:** Let's climb **PEEL** on *The Tyger*! **Point**: Blake presents the creator as terrifyingly powerful through a **semantic field** of blacksmithing.
**Mei:** **Evidence** & **Explain**: in 'In what **furnace** was thy brain?', 'furnace' connotes blinding heat, while trochaic hammer-blows enact the forging.
**Mei:** **Link**: this fills the reader with awe — or **perhaps** fear at a maker who *dares* create something so deadly!
**Narrator:** End of lesson. Six poetry traps that cost Year 8 marks every year.
**Mei:** Hooks! **SMILE**; **WHAT? HOW? WHY?**; **An iamb runs a-WAY, a trochee is a TI-ger**; and **Cool Tigers Quietly Creep, Silently Stalking Owls**!
**Nib:** One. Never stop at feature spotting, and ban 'makes the reader want to read on' — explain the exact **effect**!
**Mr H:** Two. Say '**the speaker**', not 'the poet'. The 'I' may be an invented persona.
**Kevin:** Three. Don't copy out whole stanzas! Embed **two to six** precise words inside your sentence.
**Volta:** Four. Never ignore **form and structure** — track line breaks, caesuras, and the **volta**!
**Simile:** Five. **Simile** uses *like* or *as*; **Metaphor** says it *is*; and **alliteration** is **starting** sounds only!
**Metaphor:** Six. **Free verse** is not 'anything goes' — its line breaks and pauses are still deliberate!
**Mei:** How Poems Work: **four and a half stars**! Adding 'perhaps' for an alternative reading felt very smart.
**Will:** FOUR AND A HALF?! You gave *me* four in Episode One! Wordsworth wrote about **flowers**!
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Is 'And **like** a thunderbolt he falls' a **simile** or a **metaphor**?
**Simile:** A **simile**! It compares using '**like**', keeping the eagle and the thunderbolt separate.
**Mr H:** What do we call weather or nature mirroring human emotion, as in 'The sedge has withered'?
**Nib:** **Pathetic fallacy** — a special type of personification.
**Mr H:** Does Blake's 'TY-ger TY-ger, BURN-ing BRIGHT' use **iambic** or **trochaic** rhythm?
**Metaphor:** **Trochaic** — stressed then unstressed, **DUM-da**, hammering like a blacksmith's forge!
**Mr H:** What is the difference between **enjambment** and a **caesura**?
**Kevin:** **Enjambment** runs over the end of a line without punctuation; a **caesura** is a pause **mid-line**!
**Mr H:** What is a **volta**, and where does it usually fall in a **Petrarchan** versus a **Shakespearean** sonnet?
**Volta:** The **turn** in mood or argument: at **line 9** in a Petrarchan sonnet, and usually **line 13** in a Shakespearean sonnet!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **How Poems Work** quiz in your English Lab.
**Simile:** You were **like** a star today, Metaphor!
**Metaphor:** Darling, I **AM** a star.
